prs.title: feat(git): sync branches before push and show git actions in the timeline
prs.body:
Commits, pushes, pull requests, and lands started from a thread left no record in the thread, and the agent never learned about them. A push or pull request on a branch that was behind its upstream was blocked until you rebased by hand.

- After a stacked Git action completes, the server dispatches an internal `thread.git-action.record` command. The command adds a runless `git_action` turn item that holds the action result. The payload contract is `GitActionActivityPayload` in `packages/contracts/src/git.ts`.
- The timeline shows the item as a card. You can expand the card to see each step.
- The next turn that carries a user prompt starts with a note that lists the Git actions since the last completed turn. MCP thread reads also describe the item.
- Generated commit messages now get the thread conversation for intent, as pull request text already did.
- Before a push or pull request, the server fetches the remote. It then rebases the branch onto its upstream and onto the remote default branch when either has new commits. A rebase that rewrites history pushes with `--force-with-lease`.
- **Land worktree** rebases the branch onto the base branch in the worktree before it merges, so conflicts stay in the worktree.
- A rebase that stops on conflicts stays in progress. The server asks the thread's agent to resolve it, and the action fails with a message that says so. A new action fails while a rebase is in progress.
- The git controls no longer block push or pull request when the branch is behind. A diverged branch gets a **Rebase & push** quick action.

This PR is stacked on pr/git-land-worktree because the land rebase, the land card, and the land note use its land step and its `land` result.

prs.title: feat(git): land worktree changes into the base branch
prs.body:
You had to finish a worktree thread by hand: merge, remove the worktree, then delete the branch.

- "Land" commits any changes, merges the worktree branch into its base branch in the main checkout, then removes the worktree and deletes its branch.
- Land is the default Git action for worktree threads. If you pick another commit path from the menu, the project remembers it, and that includes "Commit, push & PR".
- Land does not push. The completion toast shows the merged commit range and has a Push button. That button does not ask the default-branch question again.
- A worktree with nothing to land is cleaned up without a merge. This works even when the main checkout has uncommitted changes.
- Before it commits, land checks that the main checkout is clean and on the base branch. It fast-forwards the base branch from the remote first. It stops on conflicts or a diverged base and does not undo anything.
- After a land, the thread moves to the main checkout on the base branch.
- Progress shows the new merge and cleanup steps.

Stacked on pr/git-commit-preferences because land extends its per-project commit preference logic.

- Generated commit and PR text reads the thread's conversation, so it can explain why the change was made.

prs.title: feat(web): collapse chat history into summaries
prs.body:
A long thread gets busy, and there was no way to tidy the history you have already read.

- **Collapse history** in the chat header menu folds everything since the previous collapse into one row. The row shows "Collapsed (summarizing)" at once.
- The server asks the text generation model for a one-line summary and replaces the placeholder with it. If that fails, the row shows "Collapsed".
- You can collapse many times. Each collapse covers only what came after the previous one.
- Click a row to look inside it for the current visit. Its **×** uncollapses it for good.
- Collapses are saved with the thread. They change only the display, not what the provider sees. An agent that reads the thread through MCP sees one line that marks the collapse and gives its summary.
- The server rejects a collapse while a turn runs or when nothing new needs collapsing.

How it works:

- A collapse is a runless `history_collapse` timeline item, stored like the git-action item, so there is no migration. Its status is `running` while it summarizes, `completed` after, and `cancelled` when you uncollapse it.
- New commands: `thread.history.collapse`, `thread.history.uncollapse`, and the internal `thread.history-collapse.complete`.
- `HistoryCollapseSummaryService` runs from a `history-collapse.summarize` effect. That effect shares the per-thread lane with title generation, so it never delays provider effects.
- `generateHistorySummary` is a new text generation operation for every provider, Muse included. ACP Registry and FX do not support it.
- Clients show the menu item only when the server reports the `threadHistoryCollapse` capability.
- The thread sidebar user guide describes the feature.

Not included: the mobile app is unchanged, so it does not show or hide collapses. There is no keybinding, command palette entry, or MCP tool, and find-in-thread does not open a collapse.

Tests are in `HistoryCollapse.test.ts` and `MessagesTimeline.logic.test.ts`. I did not check it in a running app.

The base is `base/mine-4869a6f`, the parent of this commit on `mine`.

prs.title: fix(git): land branches without requiring main checkout
prs.body:
Landing a worktree failed unless the main checkout was on the base branch: "The main checkout at … is on other. Switch it to main, then land again." You had to switch branches in a checkout you were not using.

Landing now finds the worktree that has the base branch checked out, if one does:

- **No checkout has the base branch.** Landing moves the base branch ref forward. No working tree changes.
- **A checkout has the base branch.** Landing updates that checkout, as before. It refuses if that checkout has uncommitted changes, and the error names its path.
- The main checkout keeps its current branch and stays clean.
- A rebase conflict stays in the worktree being landed, as before.
- When the main checkout is not on the base branch, the success toast does not offer to push. A push from there would push the wrong branch.

Tests in `GitManager.test.ts` cover these cases: landing while main is on another branch, updating a separate checkout of main, refusing when that checkout is dirty, and keeping a conflict in the worktree.

prs.title: fix(web): size ordered list gutters to fit markers
prs.body:
In the composer, ordered list markers such as `10. ` are drawn as source text. In a monospace font a marker can be wider than the default list gutter, so it hangs to the left of the text column. In chat messages, the default `1.25rem` gutter is also too narrow for `1. ` in a monospace chat font, so a collapsed message's overflow can clip the marker.

The default `ol` gutter for chat and the composer is now `3ch`. That width fits a one-digit marker, its period, and the trailing space in any font. ChatMarkdown still widens the gutter for lists with longer markers.

prs.title: feat(web): show item runtime in work logs
prs.body:
A row in the work log did not show how long its item ran. You had to compare timestamps to find a slow command or tool call.

- A completed work log row shows its runtime to the left of the disclosure chevron, for example `850ms`, `4.2s`, or `1m 3s`. It uses the same `formatDuration` as the rest of the app.
- The runtime comes from the item's `startedAt` and `completedAt`. Any item type with both values gets the label, not only commands.
- A running item shows a live timer in the same place. The live activity row at the bottom of the timeline shows it too. The timer uses the existing `WorkingTimer`, which writes the text node directly, so React does not render the row again on each tick. `WorkingTimer` moves to `TimelineWorkEntryRow.tsx` so that both rows can use it.
- Only an item in the latest run shows the timer, and only while the thread is working. An in-progress item from a run that ended stays still.
- The hover timestamp still appears, to the left of the runtime, and the chevron does not move.
- Some rows show no runtime and no timer:
  - An interrupted item. Cleanup closes it long after it stopped, so the duration is wrong.
  - A question or an approval request. Its duration is the wait for the user, not work.
  - An item that starts and completes at the same time.

prs.title: feat(web): show remote server health in thread details
prs.body:
When a remote server felt slow, there was no way to tell from the client if the cause was the network or the server.

The thread details card now has a **Server** section for threads on a remote environment. The section does not show at the essential density. It starts collapsed. The header shows a summary such as `42 ms · CPU 37% · Mem 61%`, colored by the worst value. The open or closed state is saved in local storage.

The expanded rows, and when each turns amber / red:

| Row | Shows | Amber / red |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Round trip from the client to the server | 150 ms / 400 ms |
| CPU | Host CPU %, with core count | 70% / 90% |
| Load (1 min) | Host load average (not on Windows) | 1× / 2× cores |
| Memory | Used of total | 80% / 92% |
| Server busy | Event loop utilization of the T3 server | 50% / 80% |
| Server memory | RSS of the T3 server | none |

How it works:

- No new RPC. `HostResourcesSnapshot` gets three optional fields: `loadAverage1m`, `eventLoopUtilization`, and `serverRssBytes`. A client still decodes snapshots from older servers, and it leaves out the rows for missing fields.
- `HostResources` slept 200 ms on every read to measure CPU, so a timed request measured that sleep and not the network. It now uses the previous sample as the first reading when that sample is less than 30 seconds old. CPU and event loop use become averages over the poll interval. `useLoadBalancedEnvironment` reads the same snapshot, so it gets that average too.
- A new `hostHealth` query in `client-runtime` polls every 10 seconds while the section is mounted and times each request for latency.
- The second commit stops the summary from widening the card. The card's scroll area sizes to its content, so the summary now has zero width, grows into the free space, and truncates.

Not included: mobile. On a macOS host, each poll still starts `vm_stat`, which adds a few milliseconds to latency. No server test for the sampler change.

prs.title: fix(server): place runless items after thread history
prs.body:
On a remote server, **Collapse history** added a "Collapsed" row at the top of the thread. It hid nothing and never got a summary.

`TurnItemPositionStore` puts each turn item's ordinal in its run's range, run ordinal × 1,000,000. A runless item has no run, so it went into range 0 and sorted before every turn. On dds-dev the marker got ordinal 1, and the thread's turns used 1,000,001 to 3,000,011. The timeline hides what comes before a marker, and nothing did. The summary uses the same messages, so it was empty.

A runless item now goes into the range of the thread's latest run, after everything already in the thread. Git action rows are also runless, so this fix moves them to the correct place as well. An item with a run, or with a run ordinal from the same event batch, keeps its old placement.

This was not caught because `HistoryCollapse.test.ts` applies items straight to the projection and skips position allocation. The new `TurnItemPositionStore.test.ts` allocates positions before and after a run, and it fails without this fix.

A marker that already has a wrong ordinal keeps it. Uncollapse that marker, then collapse again.

prs.title: feat(web): show servers running in a thread workspace
prs.body:
Agents often start dev servers, databases, and other listeners in a thread's workspace. T3 Code did not show them, so you had to find the port and an address that works from your device yourself.

The thread details panel now has a collapsible "Servers" section. It lists each process that listens on a port and runs in the thread's workspace, with links or copyable addresses. The section stays hidden until the workspace has a server.

- A new `server.getWorkspaceServers` RPC takes a thread ID and needs orchestration read scope. The server resolves the directory from the thread's worktree or project root. It never accepts a path from the client, because any directory could list every server on the host.
- `WorkspaceServers` reads listeners with `lsof` on macOS, and with `ss` and `/proc` on Linux. A process belongs to the thread when its working directory is inside the workspace, or when it runs in one of the thread's T3 terminals. Windows returns `supported: false`.
- The server guesses the kind (HTTP, Postgres, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB, S3, or TCP) from the process name and port, because a probe can crash a binary protocol server. Only a guessed HTTP server gets one `GET /`. That request reads the page title, follows same-port redirects, and falls back to HTTPS when the server drops plain HTTP.
- Each server gets loopback, LAN, and tailnet addresses (MagicDNS name included) from its bind addresses. The client shows only the addresses it can reach over its connection. A local desktop sees all of them, a LAN or tailnet connection sees its own network, and a T3 Connect relay sees none. For an SSH connection, the client uses the SSH host name.
- Browsers can open HTTP, HTTPS, and S3 addresses. Database and TCP addresses copy to the clipboard.
- The client polls every 5 seconds while the section shows. The server shares one host scan between clients for 2 seconds, caches network addresses for 30 seconds, and caches page titles for 10 minutes (15 seconds when no page answered).

prs.title: feat(web): show timestamps and context usage in minimap previews
prs.body:
The timeline minimap preview showed only the message text. You could not see when a turn happened or how full the context window was at that point.

The preview now has a footer with two details:

- The time the user message was sent, in the user's timestamp format, plus its age, such as "3 minutes ago" or "4 weeks ago".
- The context usage that the turn's run ended with, as a percentage and token count, such as "Context 12% · 120k/1M". If the provider does not report a maximum, only the token count shows. If the run has no usage report, the line does not show.

prs.title: feat(web): pin the current prompt in the timeline
prs.body:
In a long turn, the prompt scrolls out of view. You then lose track of which request the agent's output answers.

When a prompt scrolls fully above the viewport, a compact copy of it now stays pinned at the top of the timeline. The copy shows at most two lines. Click it to scroll back to the prompt. As the next prompt reaches the top, it pushes the pinned copy up and then takes its place. The scroll handler sets this offset directly on the DOM, so scrolling does not re-render the timeline on each frame. The pinned prompt is hidden while find is open.

The pin is on by default. A "Pin current prompt" switch in the thread details panel turns it off for one thread. Opt-outs persist in local storage. The switch does not show for drafts or in the essential density.

prs.head: b8f26943a8b7751b4897e3543ab2f1593325691c

prs.title: fix(server): isolate thread temp files from agent memory
prs.body:
When `/tmp` is a tmpfs, systemd charges the temp files that agents write to the agents slice as shared memory. Large temp files can then cause an OOM kill of an agent, although the agent itself uses little memory.

This change gives each thread its own temp directory on disk at `<stateDir>/tmp/<thread id>`:

- `AgentScope.wrap` creates the directory with mode 0700 when it gets a `threadId`. The launch script then exports `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, and `TEMP` to point at it. The script has the same behavior with or without a systemd scope.
- The directory name is the URI-encoded thread id, with dots also encoded. The name never becomes `.` or `..`.
- If the server cannot create the directory, it logs a warning. The agent then starts with the temp directory that it inherits.
- A provider that sets its own `TMPDIR`, such as Antigravity, keeps that directory, because the provider cleans it up itself.
- A terminal on a thread uses the thread's temp directory. The new `trackScope: false` option stops the terminal from replacing the agent's scope, so `oomKilled` continues to report on the agent.
- A new `ThreadTempDirs` service removes a thread's directory when the thread is archived or deleted. At start, it also removes the directories of threads that are archived, deleted, or unknown. An unarchived thread gets a new directory at its next launch.

Tests cover the launch script exports, directory creation and naming, the provider-owned `TMPDIR` case, the terminal case, and cleanup at start and on events.

prs.title: feat(chat): suggest replies you can accept with Tab
prs.body:
After the agent finishes a turn, the user often types a short reply, such as "Yes, do that." The composer gives no help with this common step.

This change shows a suggested reply as the placeholder of the empty composer on web and desktop. Press `Tab` to put the suggestion into the composer. Press `Escape` or start to type to dismiss it.

- Claude sessions turn on the SDK's `promptSuggestions` option. The adapter stores the native suggestion for the run in the provider thread metadata. The thread shell sends it to clients, so a late suggestion updates the composer.
- Other providers use the configured text generation model through a new `thread.suggestReply` RPC and `generateReplySuggestion` operation. The prompt returns an empty reply when no clear next step exists, and it does not approve destructive actions.
- `ThreadReplySuggestionService` only suggests for the last assistant message of a completed run. It shares one in-flight request between devices and keeps a bounded cache.
- The RPC needs the orchestration operate scope. The client checks the permission on the destination environment.
- Settings > Chat > Suggest replies turns the feature off. It is on by default.
- The Claude adapter also uses the Bash tool's `description` as the intent of a command execution item.

prs.head: 240ee8a10dd5d714f56dba4be3ab93f2324b6a9e

prs.title: feat(terminal): let agents use a thread's terminals when you allow it
prs.body:
Agents cannot see or use the terminals in their own thread. The user must copy output into the chat and run commands for the agent.

This change adds an **Agent terminal access** switch to the thread's terminal panel. The switch is off by default for every thread. The grant is stored per thread in the server settings, so the user can turn it on for one thread at a time. The switch only shows when the server reports the `agentTerminalAccess` capability. A user must have permission to edit the environment's settings to change it.

When the switch is on, the thread's agent gets three MCP tools:

- `terminal_list` lists the thread's existing terminals.
- `terminal_read` returns a bounded tail of retained output. The default is 16,000 characters and the maximum is 65,536. A cursor lets the agent skip output it already has.
- `terminal_write` sends input to a running terminal. It requires full-access mode outside Plan mode, and it fails when the terminal has exited.

The tools only reach the calling thread's terminals. They never start, resize, or close a shell. The server checks the grant and a live run on every call. Writes hold the thread lock, so a revoke or mode change before the write is sent blocks it. Turning the switch off blocks further reads and input immediately. Thread cleanup removes the grant together with the terminals.

The terminal user guide now describes the switch and its limits.
